Rifaximin Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

Mechanism of action

Rifaximin is a synthetic antimicrobial which is classified as a protein synthesis inhibitor

it work by inhibiting the bacterial ability to synthesize protein

Rifaximin has a broad spectrum activity against gram positive and gram negative aerobic and anaerobic bacteria and it also work on protozoal infections such Cryptosporidiosis and blastocytosis intestinal infections

Rifaximin is non absorbable so it works only on the GI tract

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved therapeutic uses:

Reduction in risk of hepatic encephalopathy recurrence in adults

Treatment of irritable bowel syndrome associated with diarrhea in adults

Treatment of travelers’ diarrhea caused by noninvasive strains of E coli in patients older than 12

Off label therapeutic uses

In treatment of small intestine bacterial overgrowth, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, pouchitis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis , C. Difficile infection

Pharmacokinetics

it is available as an oral formula

It work locally on the GI tract and it is not absorbed into the blood

It is excreted in the feces

It is dosed between 200 mg three times a day to even 800 mg twice a day for a period between 2 to 12 weeks depending on the indication; and there is no dose adjustment in renal or liver disease and should be avoided in pregnancy (pregnancy category C)

Adverse effects

Those are limited to the GI tract due to minimal systemic absorption

they include: nausea, GI upset, fatigue , peripheral edema and muscle spasms

Long term use is associated with fungal or bacterial superinfections
